A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same research work, with readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial layout changes and the insertion of a new Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original dense and MoE training experiments, empirical scaling-law fits, benchmark accuracies, and appendix ablations and cross-dataset experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports a comparison of candidate scaling laws for model configuration in Appendix D.1.

M1.justification: The performance-prediction component for model configuration changes from a multiplicative scaling model with an interaction to an additive model without one (Equation 11). This is confined to the analytical predictor: the language-model architecture, weight-copying upcycling procedure, routing, and training losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Slimpajama-derived training data, Japanese CommonCrawl and Stack code experiments, and benchmark tasks in Table 7. The new fixed-sparsity plots redisplay existing configuration data rather than introduce another dataset or test scenario.

E2.justification: For model-configuration fitting, v2 adds comparisons against multiplicative-without-interaction and additive forms with and without interaction; v1 used the multiplicative-interaction form alone in that analysis. These alternatives already appeared in the separate dataset-size analysis. Dense/MoE, Pythia-1B, and TinyLlama-1.1B comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported training settings, validation data, benchmark metrics, and configuration-study grid are retained, including D1 = D2 = 2.3B in Section 4.2. The added functional-form comparison uses the existing leave-one-out RMS criterion. Expanded descriptions of preliminary initialization experiments do not establish changed settings or additional training runs.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.1 tests whether configuration scaling requires multiplicative structure or an interaction by comparing four candidate fits. V1 only hypothesized its selected form. Existing learning-rate, load-balancing, and data-repetition ablations remain; Figure 13 is an alternative visualization of existing observations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Leave-one-out RMS remains a measure of predictive fit; the additional RMS results do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Section 4.2 replaces exponents (0.03, 0.30, -0.01) for the old multiplicative model with (1.87, 0.34) for the additive model and updates Figure 5's predictions. Appendix D.1 newly reports RMS errors 0.0414, 0.0351, 0.0341, and 0.0322, favoring additive without interaction. These are revised fitting results, not improved language-model benchmark performance; Tables 1, 2, 7, and 8 retain their values.

T1.justification: Equation 11 substantially changes one of the principal scaling laws: a multiplicative sparsity/active-parameter expression with an interaction becomes a sum of independent power-law terms. New Appendix D.1 states separate power-law requirements and develops competing functional forms. The dataset-size law, joint scaling law, and compute-optimality derivation are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: dataset-size interactions limit upcycling efficiency, greater sparsity and active parameters improve performance, and upcycling's advantage depends on sunk cost, model size, and budget. The revised configuration formula does not change these overarching claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly interprets Japanese as harder and slower to saturate, and code as easier and faster to saturate, connecting these observations to upcycling usefulness. It also identifies data-mixture effects on downstream performance as unstudied. Sections 6–7 expand discussion of applicability to other two-stage training regimes and future theoretical and architectural extensions.

D1.justification: A new Software and Data section provides repository access information for analysis code and cross-entropy data. Appendix A.1 replaces an unspecified supplementary-script reference with concrete Megatron example links. Appendix A.6 specifies Gaussian noise, partial randomization, and low-rank substitutions within the previously mentioned preliminary experiments. Core hardware and hyperparameter disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 expands the comparison with prior additive and multiplicative transfer-learning laws and adds theoretical scaling-law, dataset-source, and vision-transformer references, including Hutter, Maloney, Lin, and Bordelon. The Branch-Train-Mix bibliography entry is removed. The main novelty positioning around dataset interactions and systematic upcycling guidance remains.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized rewriting, expanded explanations, new Software and Data and Impact Statement sections, and insertion of Appendix D, shifting the previous D/E appendices to E/F. Front matter and citation formatting also change.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, extensively resizing and repositioning figures and tables. Figure 1 gains a color bar, and new Figure 13 presents nine fixed-sparsity views of existing data. Retained appendix plots are renumbered and regrouped on the final page.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for the configuration scaling law through an explicit four-way leave-one-out comparison rather than a hypothesized form alone. Added code/data access information and clearer configuration plots improve inspectability. These gains are focused, with most experiments and principal conclusions retained. The new cross-dataset difficulty interpretation is less secure because tokenization differs, but this does not outweigh the added validation and reproducibility information.
